newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council threatens Iraq with new sanctions.
newsitem.headline: UN Council threatens Iraq with new sanctions.

text.p: The Security Council on Saturday warned Iraq it faced further sanctions for barring U.N. arms inspectors from sensitive sites by adopting a resolution worked out by U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russia's Boris Yeltsin.
The vote was a unanimous 15-0 with even China supporting the resolution after hours of consultations.

Although the agreement was weaker than the United States and Britain first proposed, both nations were satisfied that the council took a tougher position than it has over the last year. Russia had threatened to veto their original text while France would have abstained.
"There is less poison than there was before but it is still poisonous," said Iraq's ambassador Nizar Hamdoon before the vote was taken. "That's my way of describing the text."
Specifically, the resolution:

-- expresses the council's "firm intention to impose additional measures" on Iraqi officials responsible for barring the U.N. arms inspectors from sensitive sites. But new sanctions would need another council resolution.
-- suspends regular reviews, usually held every 60 days, until October 30 on the current stringent trade sanctions imposed on Iraq.
-- demands unconditional access for U.N. arms inspectors to all areas, facilities, equipment and records as well as officials and others they want to interview.

The U.N. inspectors, looking for weapons of mass destruction and related materials documents, were prevented from searching three sites earlier this month. Iraq argued it had could bar them from sites dealing with national security.
Unless the inspectors are satisfied, stringent sanctions against Iraq, particularly oil exports, cannot be lifted. The embargoes were imposed in 1990 after Baghdad invaded Kuwait.

A senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that a deal was struck on the resolution in Denver between Clinton and Yeltsin attending the Group of Seven summit of industrial nations.

The U.S. official said Yeltsin had agreed to "accept the principle of new sanctions" following his conversation with Clinton on how to prevent "rogue states seeking to develop weapons of mass destruction."

Their meeting was followed up by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright speaking to Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and French Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine. Albright, fluent in both French and Russian, did the translating, the official, said, and kept "switching from Russian to French to English."

Originally the United States and Britain wanted immediate travel sanctions on the military as well as certain government departments responsible for barring U.N. inspectors from three sensitive sites last week. But Russia, China, France and Egypt opposed punitive measures and Moscow threatened a veto.

Russia's U.N. ambassador Sergei Lavrov, denied Moscow had changed its mind, stressing repeatedly that the new text imposed no new sanctions. He said the United States and Britain had wanted to introduce a range of sanctions "that would cover even secretaries and cleaners and the like."
But he said "this resolution is to send a strong signal from the council" to make sure U.N. inspectors could complete their work and the oil embargo could be lifted.
Over the past year the council has been split on strong action against Iraq, with the United States losing ground among members of the original coalition that drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait in 1991.

The council on June 13 issued a relatively mild statement deploring a series of incidents in which U.N. inspectors said Iraqis had endangered U.N. helicopters and their crews assisting U.N. ground teams. Since then inspectors have been turned away from three sites they attempted to visit.
Chief U.N. arms inspector Rolf Ekeus had asked the council to take a firm stand.

"If Iraq is allowed now to decide what we should inspect, when we should inspect it, I think the value of the whole mechanism set up after the Gulf War would be put into question," he said, referring to the U.N. special commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping dangerous Iraqi armaments.

Ekeus, who will leave UNSCOM on July 1 and will be succeeded by Australian U.N. envoy Richard Butler, speculated it "may be because we are changing leadership that Iraq is now trying to change the ground rules somewhat."
